_comment: Factory Run 01 output. 9 shippable image-scenarios (40 coach-passed questions) authored + graded from real generated images, plus 6 queued. Each scenario maps to one image; questions reference roles/colors, never jersey numbers. Pair each with its source image before loading into the app.

questions.prompt: Look at the lone defender in gold. What did the defender just do?
options: Dove to the ice and left his feet trying to poke-check
Stayed standing in good defending position
Knocked the puck away with a successful poke-check
Skated back to help cover the goalie
questions.answer: Dove to the ice and left his feet trying to poke-check
questions.explanation: The defender committed hard and dived across the ice to try a poke-check. He missed and is now off his feet lying on the ice, no longer able to skate or defend.

questions.prompt: The defender is down on the ice. What is the puck carrier most likely to do next?
options: Skate around the fallen defender and drive to the net to shoot on the goalie
Stop and wait for the defender to get up
Pass the puck backward out of the zone
Take a long shot from far away right now
questions.answer: Skate around the fallen defender and drive to the net to shoot on the goalie
questions.explanation: Because the defender dived and is now on the ice, the path around him is opening up. The best read is to skate around him and go in alone on the goalie rather than settle for a long shot. This is the highest-percentage play, not the only legal one.

questions.prompt: Why is the defender diving to poke-check a risky choice here?
options: If he misses, he is on the ice and out of the play, leaving the lane open
It always works because the attacker can't react in time
It is the safest way to stop every rush
It forces the puck carrier to pass right away
questions.answer: If he misses, he is on the ice and out of the play, leaving the lane open
questions.explanation: A dive is all-or-nothing. The defender has committed and is now off his feet. Since he missed, he cannot recover quickly, and the path to the net opens up. Counting on a dive to always work is exactly the overconfidence that gets a defender beaten.

questions.prompt: True or False: Diving to poke-check was the right play because it was the defender's only chance to stop the rush.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: False. Diving was not his only option and it took him out of the play. A defender who stays on his feet can keep a tight gap, steer the carrier to the outside, and protect the middle. Once he dives and misses, he is off his feet and out of the play.

questions.prompt: The lone defender is the only player back against the attacking puck carrier. Spot the defender's mistake in this image.
options: He left his feet to poke-check, taking himself out of position
He committed to the carrier too early instead of forcing him to the outside first
He stayed too far back and gave up the blue line
He turned his back to the puck carrier
questions.answer: He left his feet to poke-check, taking himself out of position
questions.explanation: As the lone defender, his job is to stay on his feet, keep a tight gap, and steer the carrier to the outside. Instead he committed and dived. He missed, so now he is off his feet with the path around him opening. Committing early is a tempting wrong answer, but the precise error is leaving his feet.

questions.prompt: It's a 2-on-1. The lone defender is sitting square in the middle and hasn't committed to you or your teammate. As the puck carrier, what is the best first move?
options: Attack with speed down your lane to force the defender to commit, then take whatever he gives up
Pass right away before you even know what the defender will do
Stop and wait for the defender to make the first move
Throw the puck into the corner and chase it
questions.answer: Attack with speed down your lane to force the defender to commit, then take whatever he gives up
questions.explanation: The defender is neutral and square, so he hasn't given anything away. Attacking with speed forces a decision: if he steps to you, the pass opens; if he protects the pass, you keep the puck and shoot, and driving the net to shoot is a strong outcome too. A well-coached lone defender often tries to take the pass away and make you shoot, so read him and take what he gives.

questions.prompt: You are the puck carrier on this 2-on-1 and the defender is still square and undecided. Tap the player you should be ready to pass to if the defender steps toward you.
options: The open teammate on the other side of the defender
The spot right into the defender's stick
Your teammate only after he has skated in front of the net
The lone defender
questions.answer: The open teammate on the other side of the defender
questions.explanation: On a 2-on-1 your read is the open teammate on the far side of the defender. While the defender is neutral you stay ready to pass; the moment he commits to you, the lane opens. You do not feed the puck into the defender's stick, and you do not wait until your teammate has skated in front of the net.

questions.prompt: True or False: Because the lone defender hasn't committed yet, the puck carrier's best play is to pass across to the open teammate right now.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: False. The defender being uncommitted is exactly why you should NOT pass yet. Passing early lets the neutral defender read the puck and slide to the receiver while the goalie squares to the shot. Hold the puck, attack to make the defender pick a man, and pass only once he commits and opens the lane.

questions.prompt: Suppose the puck carrier drives at the neutral defender and the defender steps across to challenge the puck carrier. What is the best next play?
options: The passing lane to the open teammate opens — slide a firm, flat pass across for a high-percentage shot
The puck carrier should immediately turn back up the ice
The open teammate should skate behind the net out of the play
The goalie now controls both attackers by himself
questions.answer: The passing lane to the open teammate opens — slide a firm, flat pass across for a high-percentage shot
questions.explanation: Once the defender commits to the puck carrier he can no longer take away the pass, so the lane opens — that is the whole point of forcing his hand. A firm, flat pass makes the goalie move across to a new shooter, usually a better chance than shooting into a set goalie, but only AFTER the defender has truly committed.
concepts: force the goalie to move across

questions.prompt: You have the puck and skate up the ice. A defender is to your right, skating toward your path. What is happening to the space between you and that defender?
options: The space is shrinking as the defender closes in
The space is growing because you are pulling away
The space stays the same because you are matching speed
There is open ice on every side of you
questions.answer: The space is shrinking as the defender closes in
questions.explanation: The defender on your right is angling into your path, so the gap is getting smaller. Reading that the space is shrinking tells the puck carrier they need to act before the defender arrives.

questions.prompt: True or False: Based on what you can see in this picture, you have an open teammate to pass to right now.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: No teammate is visible in front of you in this picture. You are on your own facing the closing defender, so a pass is not the read here. The decision is about handling the defender and the shrinking gap yourself.

questions.prompt: You are carrying the puck up the ice and a defender is angling into your path. You glance up and see no one else around you. What is your best read in this moment?
options: Recognize it is 1-on-1 with no pass: protect the puck and change pace or angle to beat the lone defender
Pass the puck even though you do not see a teammate
Dump the puck into the corner and chase it
Stop skating and wait for the defender to take the puck
questions.answer: Recognize it is 1-on-1 with no pass: protect the puck and change pace or angle to beat the lone defender
questions.explanation: There is one defender and no support, so this is a 1-on-1. As the gap shrinks, the read is to keep the puck safe while changing your pace or angle to beat the lone defender, rather than forcing a pass that is not there or giving up possession.

questions.prompt: Tap the player who is forcing your decision by closing the gap on you.
options: The gold defender pressuring you
The puck carrier (you)
The puck on your stick
Open ice ahead of you
questions.answer: The gold defender pressuring you
questions.explanation: The gold defender skating in to close the gap is the player putting pressure on you. Identifying who is pressuring you is the first step to deciding how to attack the 1-on-1.

questions.prompt: The defender keeps closing and the gap nearly disappears. If you do nothing and keep skating straight, what is the most likely result?
options: The defender closes the gap and pressures you (challenges or angles you off)
The defender skates away and gives you open ice
You skate into the defender and lose the puck on contact, or get angled wide with no room
The play is whistled dead automatically
questions.answer: The defender closes the gap and pressures you (challenges or angles you off)
questions.explanation: With the gap shrinking and the defender actively closing, skating straight lets the defender challenge for the puck or angle you off your path. The read is to act before the gap closes by changing pace or angle.

questions.prompt: Look at the lone defender facing the puck carrier. What is the defender doing well?
options: Holding a tight gap, body in front, stick in the lane
Turned around and chasing from behind
Way too far back, giving up free space
Lunging and diving at the puck
questions.answer: Holding a tight gap, body in front, stick in the lane
questions.explanation: The defender is in good defensive posture: body squared to the carrier, a tight but controlled gap, and an active stick in the lane. That is how you defend a 1-on-1, so the picture rewards the controlled option, not chasing, gapped-out, or lunging.

questions.prompt: It is a 1-on-1 with no help nearby. What should the defender do to keep the controlled gap?
options: Stay patient, keep the gap, and steer the carrier to the outside with the stick in the lane
Rush forward and try to poke the puck right away
Stop skating and let the carrier come all the way in
Turn and skate alongside the carrier toward the net
questions.answer: Stay patient, keep the gap, and steer the carrier to the outside with the stick in the lane
questions.explanation: Because the defender already has a good gap and active stick, the job is to keep it: stay patient, maintain the tight but controlled gap (skating backward is one way), and steer the carrier outside. Lunging or turning the hips would open the lane.

questions.prompt: True or false: The lone defender is out of position and has been beaten by the puck carrier.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: False. The defender is squared up with a controlled gap and an active stick, in solid position in front of the carrier. Nothing in the image shows the carrier having gotten past him, so he has not been beaten.

questions.prompt: True or false: With no teammate visible for either side, this is an even 1-on-1, and the defender's controlled gap puts him in a good position to force the carrier wide.
options: True
False
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: True. Only one attacker and one defender are visible, so it is an even 1-on-1. With a controlled gap and an active stick, the defender is in good position to take away the inside lane and steer the carrier outside. The carrier still dictates the play with speed and fakes, so the defender must stay patient.

questions.prompt: The player with the puck has nobody in the way. It is just them and the goalie. How should they feel?
options: 😄 Happy - go score!
😟 Nervous - I have no teammates to help
😴 Sleepy - skate slowly
🤝 Wait for a friend before going in
questions.answer: 😄 Happy - go score!
questions.explanation: There are no other players in the picture, just the puck carrier and the goalie. Being alone is a good thing here. That is a breakaway, a great chance to skate in and try to score.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier has open ice all the way to the goalie and no one is chasing. What is this situation called?
options: A breakaway
A power play
A faceoff
An icing
questions.answer: A breakaway
questions.explanation: When a puck carrier skates in alone on the goalie with no defenders between them, it is a breakaway. The picture shows the attacker alone against the goalie with open ice ahead.

questions.prompt: True or false: the goalie is still sitting deep in his net.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: False. In the picture the goalie is squared to the shooter and has stepped slightly out of his crease. Coming out cuts down the angle and makes the net look smaller to the shooter.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier is alone on the goalie, who is squared up and slightly out of his net. There are no defenders chasing. What is the best next move for the puck carrier?
options: Attack with a deke or shot before any defender can catch up
Slow down to settle the puck and let the goalie reset
Turn back toward the blue line
Pass back to the point to set up a play
questions.answer: Attack with a deke or shot before any defender can catch up
questions.explanation: On a clean breakaway there are no defenders, so use the open ice and attack the goalie with a shot or deke right away. Slowing down lets the goalie set, and turning back or passing away throws away the scoring chance.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier is behind the net with the puck. The goalie is hugging the near post and a defender is on the far post. A teammate is in the slot out front. What is the best play?
options: Pass to the teammate in the slot
Jam the puck at the near post to try to squeeze it past the goalie
Stop behind the net and wait
Skate the puck back into the corner
questions.answer: Pass to the teammate in the slot
questions.explanation: The goalie is sealed to the near post and the only defender is stuck on the far post, so the teammate in the slot has the most net to shoot at and a clear lane. A pass to the slot is the highest-value option.

questions.prompt: True or false: jamming the puck in on the near side is the best chance to score here.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: The goalie is hugging the near post, so the near side is the most-defended lane and a low-percentage option. The teammate in the slot is the better play. (A near-side jam can work if the goalie over-seals and leaves a sliver, but that is not the case here.)

questions.prompt: Tap the spot that gives your team the best scoring chance from behind the net in this picture.
options: The teammate in the slot
The near post
The far post
questions.answer: The teammate in the slot
questions.explanation: Both posts are covered: the goalie owns the near post and the lone defender owns the far post. The teammate in the slot is the only unguarded scoring option, so that is the target.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier ignores the teammate in the slot and tries a wraparound to the far post. Given the defender's position, what is the MOST likely result?
options: The far-post defender breaks up the wraparound before it reaches the net
The wraparound walks in untouched for an easy goal
The goalie slides post-to-post and seals the far side before the puck arrives
The carrier beats the defender but has no angle and the puck slides across the crease unshot
questions.answer: The far-post defender breaks up the wraparound before it reaches the net
questions.explanation: A wraparound's real threat is forcing the goalie to slide post-to-post. Here, though, the defender is already set on the far post, exactly where the wraparound is headed, so the most likely result is the defender breaking it up. That is why the pass to the open slot was the stronger read.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier sees the goalie hugging the near post, then forces a wraparound into the far-post defender instead of using the teammate in the slot. What is the mistake?
options: Forcing into covered ice instead of passing to the teammate in the slot
Telegraphing the pass so the defender can jump the slot lane
Waiting too long behind the net and letting the goalie reset
Shooting low to the near side
questions.answer: Forcing into covered ice instead of passing to the teammate in the slot
questions.explanation: Both posts are covered and a teammate is open in the slot. The mistake is forcing the puck into the defender at the far post rather than making the open pass to the slot.

questions.prompt: You are the gold team, attacking in your offensive zone. The referee is about to drop the puck at the faceoff dot. Which player is responsible for taking the faceoff?
options: The center squared up opposite the other center over the dot
The winger nearest the boards
The defenseman at the point near the blue line
The winger on the far side of the circle
questions.answer: The center squared up opposite the other center over the dot
questions.explanation: By rule, the player set squarely over the dot to take the draw is the center, facing the opposing center. Wingers and defensemen set up around the circle to react once the puck is loose.

questions.prompt: You are the gold team, attacking in your offensive zone. True or false: as soon as the puck is dropped, the wingers should keep standing still and wait until the centers finish battling.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Wingers should be ready to react to a loose puck, not frozen and waiting for the centers to finish. They read the puck and support the draw, so standing still is the wrong choice.

questions.prompt: You are the gold center, attacking in your offensive zone. You win the draw cleanly. Which is one common option that opens an immediate shooting lane?
options: Win the puck back to the point player at the blue line for a shot
Push it straight ahead into the opposing center
Send it out of the zone to reset
Hard around the wall behind the opposing net
questions.answer: Win the puck back to the point player at the blue line for a shot
questions.explanation: Winning the draw back to the point is one standard offensive-zone play because the defenseman up high has a clear shooting lane. Other options can work, but among these, pulling it back to the point is the one that immediately sets up a shot.

questions.prompt: You are the gold center, attacking in your offensive zone. You lose the draw and the opposing center pulls the puck back to their own player. What is the best immediate reaction?
options: Pressure the puck carrier to disrupt the opponent's breakout from the faceoff
Freeze on the dot and watch the play develop
Coast back slowly and let your teammates handle it
Stand and look toward the bench for the next shift
questions.answer: Pressure the puck carrier to disrupt the opponent's breakout from the faceoff
questions.explanation: Faceoffs are not always won. On a lost offensive-zone draw your job is to react right away, pressuring the puck or covering your assignment, rather than freezing or quitting the play.

questions.prompt: You are the gold team, attacking in your offensive zone. One teammate is doing the wrong thing as the puck drops at the dot. Which is the mistake?
options: A winger turns and looks away from the dot as the puck is dropped
A winger steps slightly toward the boards to open a passing lane
The center keeps eyes on the puck during the draw
The point player holds position up high near the blue line
questions.answer: A winger turns and looks away from the dot as the puck is dropped
questions.explanation: Everyone near the dot needs to watch the puck so they can react the instant it is loose. A winger looking away cannot jump on a loose puck or support the center. The other actions are all reasonable, so looking away is the mistake.

questions.prompt: Two players are battling for a loose puck in the corner along the boards. What should the player do FIRST to win the battle?
options: Get body position between the opponent and the puck to protect it
Lunge for the puck with the stick before getting your body in
Tie up the opponent's stick first and worry about the puck after
Stay tall and try to muscle the opponent off with your shoulder
questions.answer: Get body position between the opponent and the puck to protect it
questions.explanation: The first job is to win body position so your body shields the puck. Lunging with the stick first leaves your body upright and easy to push off; tying up the stick ignores the loose puck; staying tall gives up the low, balanced base you need.

questions.prompt: You win the loose puck on the boards and a teammate is open in support. What is the smartest next play?
options: Protect the puck and make a controlled pass to the supporting teammate
Force the puck through the opponent's body toward the net
Curl back toward your own zone and give up the offensive-zone possession
Pass behind the net without checking where your support is
questions.answer: Protect the puck and make a controlled pass to the supporting teammate
questions.explanation: Once you have won the battle, keep the body shielding the puck and move it to support. With a teammate open, a controlled pass is the highest-percentage play. Forcing it, retreating, or passing blind give up the advantage you just earned.

questions.prompt: In this corner board battle, what body habit best lets the player keep the puck while engaged with the opponent?
options: Stay low with a wide base and keep the body between opponent and puck
Stand tall and straight to look bigger
Turn your back square to the boards so you can no longer see the ice
Lift the back skate off the ice while leaning into the opponent
questions.answer: Stay low with a wide base and keep the body between opponent and puck
questions.explanation: Winning a corner battle comes from leverage: a low, wide, balanced stance is hard to push off and keeps the body shielding the puck. Standing tall raises your center of gravity, lifting a skate sacrifices balance, and turning square to the boards leaves you blind to the ice.

questions.prompt: A player just won the puck in the corner, is under pressure from the opponent, and has a teammate available in support. Which choice is the MISTAKE to avoid?
options: Forcing the puck through the opponent's body instead of using support
Shielding the puck with the body while scanning the ice for the support option
Sealing the opponent off with a wide base, then moving the puck to support
Taking one extra stride to open a passing lane before releasing the puck
questions.answer: Forcing the puck through the opponent's body instead of using support
questions.explanation: The read rewards winning the battle and then making a smart support play, not forcing it. Driving the puck through the engaged opponent is low-percentage and the mistake here. The other options are all controlled habits that protect possession.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier is driving toward the net with a defender trying to angle him off. What is his best read?
options: Drive the net hard and read the goalie to shoot or keep going
Pass back to a trailer at the top of the circle to set up a shot
Cut across the front of the net to beat the goalie post-to-post
Slow up and protect the puck until support arrives
questions.answer: Drive the net hard and read the goalie to shoot or keep going
questions.explanation: He is already driving the net with speed. Driving hard forces the goalie to commit, which either opens shooting space or lets him keep going for a better chance. Passing back, cutting across, or slowing up all hand the defender time to close the lane.

questions.prompt: True or false: with a defender closing to angle him off, the puck carrier should slow down and let the defender catch up before deciding.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Slowing down gives the defender time to close the lane and the goalie time to set. The puck carrier should act quickly, driving the net to force the goalie to commit and then shooting or continuing the drive.

questions.prompt: The puck carrier is driving the net and the goalie is giving up space. What happens next if he reads it well?
options: He attacks the space the goalie gives up, shooting into it or driving closer to finish
He fakes the shot, freezes the goalie, then loops back to the blue line to reset
He throws it blindly off the goalie's pads and hopes for a bounce
He stops at the top of the circle and waits for a teammate to open up
questions.answer: He attacks the space the goalie gives up, shooting into it or driving closer to finish
questions.explanation: Reading where the goalie gives up space is the whole point of the drive. A good read means attacking that opening, either shooting into it or continuing the drive to finish. Looping back, throwing it blindly, or stopping all waste the chance.

questions.prompt: Same net drive, with a defender angling him off. Which choice by the puck carrier would be the mistake?
options: Veering wide to the boards away from the net
Driving hard to force the goalie to commit
Reading the goalie before deciding to shoot or keep driving
Protecting the puck from the angling defender while staying on the net
questions.answer: Veering wide to the boards away from the net
questions.explanation: He has a live drive on the net and is in position to read the goalie. Bailing wide to the boards hands the defender the angle and removes the scoring chance the drive created. The right play is to keep attacking the net, protect the puck, and read the goalie.

queued.reason: Isolated 1-on-1 with a square, neutral defender and no teammate; no single clearly-best play.
Near-duplicate of tile-10; low teaching value.
Puck and player roles not clearly readable; supports multiple defensible reads.
Unclear puck possession; no clean single read.
Too cluttered to support a clean, fair read.
